claims.claim: Wolfe writes in his foreword to Soldier of the Mist that the narrator recorded place names as he believed he understood their meanings, so the record's names are the narrator's guesses.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, foreword to Soldier of the Mist (Tor, 1986), p. xii, quoted by Scott Wowra in Ultan's Library, 7 September 2016
claims.quote: he understood (or believed he understood) their meanings

claims.claim: Wowra finds that folk etymology, a plausible but wrong translation, is the main way Wolfe's amnesiac narrator generates the place names in his record.
claims.source: Scott Wowra, 'Place Names in Gene Wolfe's Soldier of the Mist', Ultan's Library, 7 September 2016
claims.quote: it is the primary method Latro uses to record his place names

claims.claim: Wolfe says in a 1988 interview that his narrator arrives at the right meaning of a city's name by an incorrect derivation.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Darrell Schweitzer, Weird Tales, Spring 1988, quoted by Scott Wowra in Ultan's Library, 7 September 2016
claims.quote: although his derivation of it is incorrect

claims.claim: Wowra describes Wolfe's toponyms in Soldier of the Mist as plain compounded names such as Hundred Eyed and Redface Island that provoke wonder and puzzlement.
claims.quote: awash with charming place names that evoke wonder and puzzlement

claims.claim: Wolfe explains in his introduction that his narrator named a region Silent Country after mishearing a remark about a person's laconic manners.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, introduction to Soldier of the Mist (Tor, 1986), p. xii, quoted by Scott Wowra in Ultan's Library, 7 September 2016
claims.quote: seems to have heard some taciturn person referred to as

claims.claim: Wowra concludes that the record's place names are dominated by folk etymology, with descriptive, associative and commemorative naming used less often.
claims.quote: Latro relies predominantly on folk etymology

claims.claim: Gevers argues that Wolfe writes so that any seemingly incidental paragraph reflects the whole design, which is what obliges the reader to read incidental detail as evidence.
claims.source: Nick Gevers, 'The Reader as Augur: Beginnings and Endings in Gene Wolfe's The Book of the Long Sun', written 1998, published in Ultan's Library, 5 September 2000
claims.quote: every paragraph, however incidental seeming, reflects the whole

claims.claim: Gevers argues that the divination scenes inside The Book of the Long Sun function as instruction to the reader in how closely the text must be read.
claims.source: Nick Gevers, 'The Reader as Augur', Ultan's Library, 5 September 2000
claims.quote: instruction in, the demands of incisive reading

claims.claim: Gevers finds that every volume of The Book of the Long Sun opens with a dialogue in which the informed party releases what he knows only in oracular or obscure form.
claims.source: Nick Gevers, 'The Reader as Augur', Ultan's Library, 5 September 2000
claims.quote: which he will only yield up in oracular or otherwise obscure form

claims.claim: Gevers describes Wolfe's narration in the final volume of the Long Sun as spare and unexplanatory, made of hints and implications.
claims.source: Nick Gevers, 'The Reader as Augur', Ultan's Library, 5 September 2000
claims.quote: narration becomes spare, unexplanatory, a minefield of hints and implications

claims.claim: Gevers uses Kim Stanley Robinson and John Clute's term slingshot ending for a close whose implications carry past the end of the text.
claims.source: Nick Gevers, 'The Reader as Augur', Ultan's Library, 5 September 2000
claims.quote: an ending whose momentum of implication carries well beyond the confines

claims.claim: Gevers notes that the narrator of The Book of the Long Sun identifies himself only in the last pages, which forces the reader to re-appraise everything already read.
claims.source: Nick Gevers, 'The Reader as Augur', Ultan's Library, 5 September 2000
claims.quote: thus forcing the reader to re-appraise the whole of the preceding text

claims.claim: Gevers states that Wolfe's third volume instructs the reader to assemble the meaning of the text out of clues that appear disconnected.
claims.source: Nick Gevers, 'The Reader as Augur', Ultan's Library, 5 September 2000
claims.quote: assembling the meaning of the text from numerous seemingly disconnected clues

claims.claim: Borski endorses Wright's finding that the absence of any discourse between coloniser and colonised in The Fifth Head of Cerberus destabilises the reality the book reports.
claims.source: Robert Borski, 'Desanctifying Victor Trenchard', Ultan's Library, 24 May 2002 (dated December 2001)
claims.quote: the destabilizing effects such omissions have on reality

claims.claim: Borski links two of Wolfe's characters into a single pattern using small domestic repetitions, among them the barley soup each is served in prison.
claims.source: Robert Borski, 'Desanctifying Victor Trenchard', Ultan's Library, 24 May 2002
claims.quote: Both men are served barley soup while imprisoned
